title: Customization profiles and safe composition strategies for VPC IaC
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: Customers require per-tenant customizations for Private (VPC) deployments without forking the core Terraform modules. Existing approaches (full module forks, ad-hoc per-customer branches) increase maintenance and make upgrades risky. We need a repeatable, testable pattern that supports:
- non-destructive per-customer overrides
- safe module upgrades with canary/staged rollouts
- composable variables and small patch overlays that are easy to review
- integrated health checks and preflight validations to avoid bad applies

Proposal summary: Introduce "customization profiles" — composable overlay artifacts that describe only the delta between Redwood's reference modules and the customer-specific layout. Profiles are applied at plan/apply time via a composition layer that:
1) resolves a base module manifest (from Redwood's module registry)
2) loads zero-or-more profile overlays (yaml or hcl partials) for per-customer quirks
3) performs a deterministic transformation (patch/merge) into a transient working module tree
4) runs static validation, contract tests, and health-check preflight hooks before apply

Key patterns and implementation details: 
- Overlay format: YAML-based patches with allowed operations: set, append, remove, merge. Keep overlays small (max ~200 lines). Overlays point to a "profile schema" that is validated by CI.
- Variable surface: Introduce a single "profile" input that references an overlay id and a small set of guardrails (region, instance_class_overrides, allowed_cidrs). Avoid exposing raw provider-level overrides where possible.
- Module composition: Core modules expose well-defined extension points (input maps and lifecycle hooks). Implement a lightweight composition tool (go binary in infra-ci) that materializes the composed module into a temporary directory and outputs terraform-compatible files.
- Remote state and isolation: By default keep per-customer remote state backends (S3/GCS buckets with unique prefixes). Profiles may opt into shared state only with an explicit "shared_state" flag and approval.
- Upgrade safety: 
  * Version pinning: each profile pins the module major.minor. Upgrades require an explicit profile migration.
  * Canary applies: CI supports running applies against a small canary sandbox (customer staging) first. The orchestration pipeline will promote changes after health checks pass.
  * Preflight hooks: run terraform plan -> diff checker -> policy enforcement -> smoke apply (or dry-run apply where supported). Failure blocks promotion.
- Health checks & runtime probes: Profiles may register a "post-apply" healthcheck manifest which runs a set of probes (http, tcp, grpc, and custom runtime assertions against the Redwood runtime API). Healthchecks return structured results consumed by the rollout controller.
- Rollback & drift detection: Keep apply run artifacts and last-known-good plans serialized in object storage. If a healthcheck fails post-apply, automation triggers rollback by re-applying the last-known-good plan. Also schedule periodic drift detection runs that compare live resource state to composed manifests.
- Security & policy: Integrate with policy-as-code (OPA/Sentinel) in the pipeline. Profiles flagged with high-risk changes require manual approval (label + approver list) and audit logging.

Tradeoffs and rationale: 
- Benefits: small overlays reduce merge churn, upgrades are scoped and reviewable, and canary flows reduce blast radius.
- Costs: requires additional tooling (composition binary + validation harness) and CI complexity. Some customers will still request direct forks for extreme customization; we should treat fork requests as a last resort.

Deliverables (MVP):
- composition tool (go) that materializes overlays into terraform files
- overlay schema, validators, and example overlays for 3 customers
- CI pipeline jobs: compose -> plan -> policy -> canary-apply -> healthchecks -> promote
- documentation and a migration guide for existing customers

Success metrics: 
- reduce per-customer fork count by 80% within 3 months after rollout
- 90% of upgrades use automated canary path successfully
- zero customer-impacting failed upgrades in first 6 months (measured by post-apply rollbacks)
